mainTopic: An ox that kills a free man or a slave: admission, accidental killing, כופר and the thirty שקלים, and liability for killing minors
overview: רבה explains why an owner who admits that his ox killed a free man pays the victim's value (דמים), while an owner who admits that his ox killed a slave pays nothing. For a free man, admission can obligate כופר, but the thirty שקלים for a slave are a קנס, and a קנס is never paid through one's own admission. רב שמואל בר רב יצחק challenges this from a ברייתא. The ברייתא is then reread so that it only covers cases proven by witnesses. רבא asks whether a fire that kills someone by accident should also pay דמים. The גמרא tests two possible sources for his view, rejects both, and leaves the question as תיקו. רבי יוחנן learns from the extra word 'אם' that כופר is paid even for an accidental killing, and also that the thirty שקלים are paid for a slave killed by accident. ריש לקיש exempts the accidental slave case but agrees about כופר, because only the 'אם' in the payment clause is extra. Finally, a ברייתא learns that an ox's owner is liable for killing children just as for adults, and asks whether logic could have taught this. Its קל וחומר continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Free man: admission can obligate ransom, so without witnesses he pays value
steps.stepSummary: For a free victim there is a case where the owner pays כופר based on his own admission. So when there are no witnesses, he still pays דמים.
steps.simpleTranslation: However, with a free man, there is a case where the owner pays ransom based on his own word. What is the case? Witnesses came and testified that the ox killed, but they don't know whether it was a תם or a מועד. The owner says it was a מועד, so he pays ransom based on his own word. Therefore, where there are no witnesses, he pays the victim's value.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה continues explaining why a free victim and a slave victim are treated differently. He starts with the free man and shows that the owner's own admission can make him pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only a מועד ox's owner pays כופר. If witnesses saw the killing but did not know the ox's status, the owner's admission 'it was a מועד' makes him pay כופר, because כופר is atonement and not a fine. Since admission works for a free man, רבה rules that even with no witnesses at all, the admitting owner pays דמים.

keyTerms.meaning: A free person (not a slave)
Ransom paid by the owner of a מועד ox that killed a person
Based on his own admission
An ox with no history of goring
An ox already warned as a habitual gorer
The monetary value of the victim

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two cases. The witness case is only the 'proof' scenario showing that admission can obligate כופר. רבה's actual ruling is about the case with no witnesses, where the owner pays דמים.

phrases.english: However, with a free man,
where one pays ransom based on his own admission –
and what is the case?

phrases.aramaic: דְּאִי אֲתוֹ סָהֲדֵי וְאַסְהִידוּ בֵּיהּ דִּקְטַל,
phrases.english: if witnesses came and testified about it that it killed,

phrases.aramaic: וְלָא יָדְעִי אִי תָּם הֲוָה אִי מוּעָד הֲוָה,
phrases.english: but they do not know whether it was innocuous or forewarned,
and its owner said that it is forewarned,
he pays ransom based on his own admission –
so where there are no witnesses, he pays the value;

steps.triggerLanguage: מִיהוּ, בֶּן חוֹרִין דִּמְשַׁלֵּם כּוֹפֶר עַל פִּי עַצְמוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רבה's statement from the previous amud, explaining the free-man side of his distinction.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For a free victim, admission can obligate כופר, so without witnesses the admitting owner pays דמים.

steps.title: Slave: admission never obligates the fine, so without witnesses no value is paid
steps.stepSummary: For a slave victim, the thirty-shekel payment is a קנס, which is never paid through one's own admission. So without witnesses, the owner does not pay דמים.
steps.simpleTranslation: But with a slave, the owner does not pay the fine based on his own word. What is the case? Witnesses came and testified that the ox killed, but they don't know whether it was a תם or a מועד. The owner says it was a מועד, yet he does not pay the fine based on his own word. Therefore, where there are no witnesses, he does not pay the value.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה finishes his distinction by showing the slave side. Here admission does not obligate payment, so there is no payment without witnesses either.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The thirty shekels for a slave is a קנס. There is a rule that a person does not pay a קנס based on his own admission, so even the owner's claim 'it was a מועד' does not obligate him. Because admission cannot obligate payment for a slave, רבה rules that with no witnesses the owner does not pay דמים. This mirrors step 1 exactly, but with the opposite result.

keyTerms.meaning: A (Canaanite) slave
A fixed penalty payment. Here, the thirty shekels for a slave.
Regarding / in the case of

steps.whatToRemember: רבה's rule: wherever admission can obligate the main payment (כופר for a free man), admission without witnesses obligates דמים. Where it cannot (קנס for a slave), there are no דמים.

phrases.english: Regarding a slave,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְשַׁלֵּם קְנָס עַל פִּי עַצְמוֹ –
phrases.english: where one does not pay a fine based on his own admission –
phrases.notes: The fine here is the thirty shekels the Torah sets for a slave killed by an ox.

phrases.english: and what is the case?

phrases.aramaic: דְּאִי אֲתוֹ עֵדִים וְאַסְהִידוּ בֵּיהּ דִּקְטַל,
phrases.english: if witnesses came and testified about it that it killed,

phrases.aramaic: וְלָא יָדְעִי אִי תָּם הֲוָה אִי מוּעָד הֲוָה,
phrases.english: but they do not know whether it was innocuous or forewarned,
and its owner said it is forewarned –

phrases.aramaic: לָא מִשְׁתַּלַּם קְנָס עַל פִּי עַצְמוֹ.
phrases.english: the fine is not paid based on his own admission.

phrases.aramaic: הֵיכָא דְּלֵיכָּא עֵדִים – לָא מְשַׁלֵּם דָּמִים.
phrases.english: So where there are no witnesses – he does not pay the value.

steps.triggerLanguage: גַּבֵּי עֶבֶד, שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְשַׁלֵּם קְנָס עַל פִּי עַצְמוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the contrast begun in step 1, giving the opposite result for a slave.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For a slave victim, admission cannot obligate the קנס, so without witnesses the admitting owner does not pay דמים.

steps.title: A ברייתא equates slave and free man
steps.stepSummary: רב שמואל בר רב יצחק cites a ברייתא: whatever makes one liable for a free man makes one liable for a slave, both for כופר and for the ox's death.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שמואל בר רב יצחק raised an objection: Whenever one is liable for a free man, he is liable for a slave, both in ransom and in death.
steps.whatsHappening: רב שמואל בר רב יצחק brings a ברייתא to challenge רבה. This step quotes the source and sets up the attack in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says the liability for a slave matches the liability for a free man in every scenario. That seems to clash with רבה's claim that the two cases differ. The exact force of the challenge depends on what 'כופר' means for a slave, which the next step explains.

keyTerms.meaning: Any case where one is liable
Death. Here, the ox being stoned.

steps.confusionAlert: 'מיתה' here means the ox is put to death, not the owner.

phrases.aramaic: מֵתִיב רַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר רַב יִצְחָק:
phrases.english: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzḥak raised an objection:
Whoever is liable for a free man –
is liable for a slave,
both regarding ransom and regarding death.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵתִיב רַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר רַב יִצְחָק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא against רבה's distinction between free man and slave.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's ruling that an owner who admits to his ox killing a slave pays no דמים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא treats slave and free man equally in payment liability, which seems to contradict רבה's distinction.

steps.title: Ransom for a slave must mean value
steps.stepSummary: There is no real כופר for a slave, so the ברייתא must mean דמים. That contradicts רבה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is there ransom for a slave?! Rather, doesn't it mean the value?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sharpens the objection. 'כופר' cannot mean real ransom for a slave, so it must mean paying the value, which goes against רבה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For a slave, the Torah requires thirty shekels, not כופר. So the ברייתא's word 'כופר' must refer to a payment of value (דמים) that applies to both. If the owner pays דמים for a slave just as for a free man, then רבה's claim that there are no דמים for a slave seems wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: Is there such a thing?! (a rhetorical question)
Rather, is it not... (introduces the forced reading)

steps.whyThisMatters: The challenge works by re-reading one word ('כופר') in the ברייתא as 'דמים.' This sets up the answer the גמרא must give next.

phrases.english: Is there ransom for a slave?!
Rather, is it not the value?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how the ברייתא quoted in step 3 actually contradicts רבה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's ruling in step 2 that no דמים are paid for a slave without witnesses
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Since real כופר does not exist for a slave, the ברייתא's 'כופר' must mean דמים, so דמים are paid for a slave just as for a free man.

steps.title: Rereading the ברייתא so it fits רבה
steps.stepSummary: Either רב שמואל בר רב יצחק himself, or רבה, answers the challenge. The ברייתא is read as two parallel cases, and both need עדים. With an intentional goring there is כופר for a free man and קנס for a slave. With an unintentional killing there is דמים for both.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say רב שמואל בר רב יצחק raised the challenge and also answered it. Others say רבה answered him. This is what the ברייתא means: In any case where the owner pays כופר for a free man, meaning the ox killed on purpose and עדים saw it, he pays the קנס for a slave. In any case where the owner pays דמים for a free man, meaning the ox killed by accident and עדים saw it, he also pays דמים for a slave, again by accident and through עדים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 4 by explaining what the ברייתא really means. Every case in the ברייתא is a case where עדים saw what happened.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge in Step 4 assumed the ברייתא made the slave's דמים match the free man's דמים in every situation, including when the owner admits on his own. This answer limits the comparison to cases with עדים: an unintentional killing with עדים brings דמים for both. So the ברייתא never says the owner pays for a slave based on his own admission, and רבה's rule from Step 2 stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Raises a challenge and resolves it himself
Intentionally (the ox meant to kill this person)
Unintentionally (the ox did not mean to kill this person)
Through the testimony of witnesses

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read this as saying a slave has no כופר at all and that is the end of it. The ברייתא's 'כופר' for a slave means the fixed קנס of thirty שקלים. The 'דמים' half covers only accidental killings that עדים saw, never a case based on the owner's own admission.

phrases.english: There are those who say:

phrases.aramaic: הוּא מוֹתֵיב לַהּ וְהוּא מְפָרֵק לַהּ,
phrases.english: he raised the challenge and he resolved it,
phrases.notes: 'He' is רב שמואל בר רב יצחק, who brought the ברייתא in Step 3.

phrases.english: and there are those who say: רבה said to him:
this is what it teaches:
any case where one is liable for a free man
intentionally, through witnesses, to pay ransom,
he is liable for a slave to pay a fine.
And any case where one is liable for a free man

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁלֹּא בְּכַוָּונָה עַל פִּי עֵדִים, דָּמִים –
phrases.english: unintentionally, through witnesses, to pay value,
he is liable for a slave

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁלֹּא בְּכַוָּונָה עַל פִּי עֵדִים, דָּמִים.
phrases.english: unintentionally, through witnesses, to pay value.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in Step 4 by rereading the ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the source: the ברייתא is limited to cases established by witnesses
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא makes a slave's דמים equal to a free man's in every case, even when the owner admits on his own.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא pairs intentional goring (כופר and קנס) with unintentional killing (דמים and דמים), and in both pairs the facts come through עדים, so there is no payment for a slave based on admission.

steps.title: רבא: Then an accidental fire should pay דמים too
steps.stepSummary: רבא challenges רבה: if an ox that kills by accident brings דמים, a person whose fire kills someone by accident, with עדים, should also pay דמים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to רבה: If so, then when a person's fire kills someone by accident and עדים saw it, he should also pay the victim's value!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks the answer from Step 5. He takes the idea that an accidental killing brings דמים and applies it to damage done by fire.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 said an unintentional killing with עדים brings דמים, even though no כופר is paid. רבא argues that the same logic should require דמים when someone's fire accidentally kills a person. He assumes that in the fire case no such payment is made, so the reading in Step 5 seems to prove too much.

keyTerms.meaning: If so (introduces a problem that follows from what was just said)
His fire (damage done by a fire a person started)
Let him pay (said as a challenge: he should pay!)

phrases.english: רבא said to him:
If so,
with his fire, unintentionally,
through witnesses, let him pay value!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reading in Step 5 by extending its logic to fire.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 5 that an unintentional killing through witnesses brings דמים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If an accidental killing by an ox brings דמים, an accidental killing by fire should too. רבא assumes fire does not pay in that case, so the reading leads to a wrong result.

steps.title: How does רבא know fire does not pay?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא stops to ask what source tells רבא that someone whose fire kills a person by accident does not pay דמים.
steps.simpleTranslation: And how does רבא know that he does not pay?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses to check the assumption behind רבא's challenge. This question sets up the next step, where the גמרא looks for רבא's source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's challenge only works if fire really does not pay דמים for an accidental killing. The גמרא wants to find where that rule comes from before accepting the challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: And from where does he know? (asks for someone's source)
Pays

phrases.english: And from where does רבא know
that he does not pay?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Examines the hidden assumption in רבא's challenge from Step 6.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source for רבא's assumption that a person whose fire kills someone by accident does not pay דמים.

steps.title: A first try: the משנה of the bound slave and the goat
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests רבא's source might be a משנה about a fire. If a goat was tied next to the fire and a slave was nearby, the one who set the fire is liable. If the slave was tied and the goat was nearby, he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: Maybe the source is what we learned in a משנה: If a goat was tied next to it and a slave was near it, and they burned together with it, he is liable. If a slave was tied next to it and a goat was near it, and they burned together with it, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a possible source for רבא's rule: a משנה about a fire that burned a goat and a slave. The word אילימא tells us this is only a first suggestion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the second case of the משנה, a slave who was tied up and could not escape was burned, and the one who set the fire is exempt. The suggestion is that this shows no payment for a person killed by fire, which would support רבא's assumption. The opening word אילימא hints that the גמרא may go on to reject this source.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (offers a suggestion that may later be rejected)
From what we learned in a משנה
Tied up (unable to run away)
Near, next to (but not tied)
Young goat

steps.confusionAlert: Notice which one is tied in each case. When the goat is tied, he is liable. When the slave is tied and cannot escape, he is exempt.

phrases.english: If we say it is from what we learned:
there was a goat tied next to it,
phrases.notes: 'It' is the stack of grain that was set on fire, in the משנה on דף סא.

phrases.english: and a slave near it,
and it was burned with it, he is liable.
A slave tied next to it,
and a goat near it,
and it was burned with it, he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a first possible answer to the question in Step 7.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's assumption that a person whose fire kills someone does not pay דמים
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה on דף סא: when the slave is tied and the goat is near, and both are burned, the one who set the fire is exempt.

steps.title: The goat-and-slave משנה is no proof
steps.stepSummary: The proof from the fire משנה fails. ריש לקיש explained that the משנה is talking about someone who set fire to the slave's body directly. He is exempt from paying only because he gets the death penalty, which is the bigger punishment.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't ריש לקיש say that the משנה is talking about a case where he set fire to the slave's own body? He is exempt only because he receives the greater punishment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof from step 8. It says the משנה exempts the fire-setter for a different reason, not because fire never pays דמים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 8, the משנה seemed to say that a fire that kills a slave brings no payment. ריש לקיש explains that this is a case where the person directly burned the slave, so he is a murderer facing the death penalty. A person who faces death does not also pay money. The exemption therefore says nothing about an accidental killing by fire.

keyTerms.meaning: He set fire to
He receives the greater punishment, so he is exempt from the smaller one (paying money)

phrases.english: But didn't ריש לקיש say:
for example, where he set fire to the body of the slave itself,
so he receives the greater punishment of the two!
phrases.notes: The greater punishment here is the death penalty for killing the slave. Because he gets that, he does not also have to pay.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof offered in step 8.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the משנה as a source for רבא's claim that accidental fire killing brings no דמים.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The משנה's exemption comes from קם ליה בדרבה מיניה in a case of direct burning, not from a rule about accidental fire.

steps.title: A second suggested source: the fire-versus-pit ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests another source: a ברייתא that lists how fire is stricter than a pit. The ברייתא mentions that fire is liable even for things it would not normally burn. It does not mention that fire pays דמים for an accidental killing, which hints that fire does not pay it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the source is the ברייתא that says: fire is stricter than a pit, because fire counts as forewarned to burn both things fit for it and things not fit for it, which is not so with a pit. But it does not teach that fire pays דמים for an unintentional killing, unlike a pit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a new source for רבא. It points to what a ברייתא leaves out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא lists the ways fire is stricter than a pit. If fire paid דמים for an accidental killing, that would also be a stricter rule, and the ברייתא should have listed it. Since the ברייתא does not list it, maybe fire does not pay דמים in that case.

keyTerms.meaning: A stricter rule, a way one case is more severe
Fire, one of the main categories of damage
Pit, another main category of damage
Considered forewarned, so the owner is fully responsible
It does not teach (the source leaves this out)

phrases.english: Rather, from that which was taught in a ברייתא:
There is a stricter rule for fire than for a pit:
that fire is considered forewarned to consume
both something that is fit for it
and something that is not fit for it,
phrases.notes: Fit for it means things that burn easily. Not fit for it means things that don't.

phrases.english: which is not so with a pit.
But that fire pays
the value for an unintentional killing –

phrases.aramaic: מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בְּבוֹר, לָא קָתָנֵי!
phrases.english: which is not so with a pit, it does not teach!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first source was rejected, a new source is proposed for the question in step 7.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's assumption that a person whose fire kills someone by accident does not pay דמים.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of חומר באש מבבור, which is silent about fire paying דמים for an unintentional killing.

steps.title: The ברייתא may have left things out
steps.stepSummary: The proof from the ברייתא fails. A ברייתא does not have to list every difference, so leaving something out proves nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps the ברייתא taught some differences and left others out?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof from the ברייתא's silence.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof in step 10 depended on the ברייתא listing every way fire is stricter than a pit. The גמרא answers that a ברייתא can teach one point and skip others. So the missing rule about accidental killing proves nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: Perhaps
It taught some things and left some out

phrases.english: Perhaps it taught some differences and left others out?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof offered in step 10.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the ברייתא as a source for רבא.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A proof from silence does not work, because the ברייתא may not list every difference (תנא ושייר).

steps.title: רבא was really asking a question
steps.stepSummary: Since no source is found, the גמרא concludes that רבא was not challenging רבה. He himself was unsure: does a person whose fire kills someone by accident pay דמים or not?
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא himself was unsure about this: if a person's fire kills someone unintentionally, does he pay דמים, or not?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא wraps up this section. It says רבא's words in step 6 were a question he was unsure about, not an attack on רבה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both suggested sources were rejected, so רבא had no proof that accidental fire killing is exempt. The גמרא therefore reads his statement as a question he did not know the answer to. That means רבה's view, that an ox which kills by accident brings דמים, is no longer challenged.

keyTerms.meaning: Himself
He was unsure about it (it was a question for him)
Unintentionally, by accident

steps.whatToRemember: No source was found that accidental fire killing is exempt from דמים. רבא's words were not a challenge to רבה but a question that רבא himself was unsure about.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think רבא disproved רבה. In the end, רבא's statement is treated as his own open question, so רבה's position still stands.

phrases.english: Rather, רבא himself
was unsure about it:
if his fire killed someone unintentionally –
does he pay the value, or not?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא רָבָא גּוּפֵיהּ אִבְּעוֹיֵי מִבַּעְיָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After both sources fail, the גמרא re-reads רבא's challenge from step 6 as an open question.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבא was not challenging רבה. He was unsure whether a person whose fire kills someone by accident pays דמים, so רבה's position is not disproved.

steps.title: Laying out both sides of רבא's question about fire
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the two possible ways to think about a fire that kills a person by accident: compare it to an ox, or treat it differently.
steps.simpleTranslation: Do we say that only with an ox, which pays כופר when it kills on purpose, does the owner pay דמים when it kills by accident? But fire, which never pays כופר even when it kills on purpose, would not pay דמים by accident either? Or maybe we say: an ox pays דמים by accident even though there is no כופר, so fire should also pay דמים by accident, even though it never pays כופר?
steps.whatsHappening: Now that we know רבא was really asking a question, the גמרא lays out both sides of it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Side one: paying דמים for an accidental killing is a 'replacement' for כופר. So it only applies where כופר exists, like an ox, and not to fire. Side two: paying דמים is its own separate obligation, and it does not depend on כופר. So fire would pay it too.

keyTerms.meaning: Ransom money the owner of a known goring ox pays when it kills a person
The money value of the person who was killed
His fire (damage caused by a fire he set)
Or perhaps (introduces the second side of a question)
At least, in any case

phrases.english: Do we say: it is only regarding an ox
that, since when it kills on purpose he pays ransom,
when it kills by accident he pays the value;

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל אִשּׁוֹ, דִּבְכַוָּונָה לָא מְשַׁלֵּם כּוֹפֶר –
phrases.english: but his fire, which even on purpose does not pay ransom,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁלֹּא בְּכַוָּונָה נָמֵי לָא מְשַׁלֵּם דָּמִים;
phrases.english: by accident also does not pay the value;

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא, כֵּיוָן דְּגַבֵּי שׁוֹרוֹ שֶׁלֹּא בְּכַוָּונָה –
phrases.english: or perhaps, since regarding his ox by accident,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּב דְּלֵיכָּא כּוֹפֶר, מְשַׁלֵּם דָּמִים;
phrases.english: even though there is no ransom, he pays the value;
regarding his fire also,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּב דִּבְכַוָּונָה לָא מְשַׁלֵּם כּוֹפֶר,
phrases.english: even though on purpose he does not pay ransom,
by accident at least he should pay the value?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the question that step 12 said רבא was unsure about
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does paying דמים for an accidental killing depend on there being כופר in that kind of case, or is it a separate obligation that fire also has?

steps.title: The question stays unresolved
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא admits it does not know the answer. The question is left as תיקו.
steps.simpleTranslation: We do not know. Let it stand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the question about fire without an answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No source settled the question (steps 8–11), and logic could go either way (step 13). So it is left open.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Let it stand' — the question stays unresolved
We know

steps.whatToRemember: Whether a fire that kills someone by accident makes its owner pay דמים is an unresolved question (תיקו).

phrases.english: And we do not know; let it stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the question laid out in step 13
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The question about fire is left as תיקו.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: an ox that kills by accident still pays כופר
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי reports that רבי יוחנן learns from the extra word 'אם' that כופר is paid even for an accidental killing by an ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב דימי came, he said in the name of רבי יוחנן: the פסוק could have just said 'כפר'. Why does it say 'אם כפר'? To include כופר for an accidental killing, the same as כופר for a killing on purpose.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new opinion. It disagrees with רבה, who said an ox that kills by accident does not pay כופר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן treats the word 'אם' as extra, and an extra word comes to teach something. He says it adds the accidental case. So for רבי יוחנן, כופר applies in both cases, on purpose and by accident.

keyTerms.meaning: When he came (from ארץ ישראל to בבל)
Why does the פסוק say this? (points to an extra word)
To include

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a direct disagreement with רבה's ruling, which this whole discussion has been built on.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי אֲתָא רַב דִּימִי, אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: When Rav Dimi came, he said in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan:
'A ransom' would be enough; why does the verse say 'If a ransom'?
To include ransom for an accidental killing,
just like ransom for a killing on purpose.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתָא רַב דִּימִי, אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to רבה's ruling about the ox and brings an opinion that disagrees with it
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An ox that kills a person by accident still makes its owner pay כופר, learned from the extra word 'אם'.

steps.title: אביי: then the slave case should work the same way
steps.stepSummary: אביי argues that the same reading of 'אם עבד' would make the owner pay thirty שקלים for a slave killed by accident. But ריש לקיש rules that he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: If so, the slave case should work the same way. Why does the פסוק say 'אם עבד'? To include a slave killed by accident, the same as one killed on purpose! And if you say that is true, didn't ריש לקיש say that an ox that killed a slave by accident is exempt from thirty שקלים?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי challenges רבי יוחנן's reading by applying the same method to the slave פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The slave פסוק also starts with 'אם'. So if 'אם' adds the accidental case for כופר, it should add the accidental case for the thirty שקלים too. But ריש לקיש rules that there is no payment for a slave killed by accident. So the method seems to give a result that goes against ריש לקיש's ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: If so, then... (pushes an idea to a result that seems wrong)
And if you say that is indeed so
Thirty שקלים, the fixed payment for a slave killed by an ox

steps.confusionAlert: אביי is not saying the accidental slave case pays. He is saying רבי יוחנן's method would force it to pay, which goes against ריש לקיש.

phrases.english: Abaye said to him: If so,

phrases.aramaic: עֶבֶד נָמֵי – מָה תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר ״אִם עֶבֶד״?
phrases.english: a slave also: why does the verse say 'If a slave'?

phrases.aramaic: לְרַבּוֹת עֶבֶד שֶׁלֹּא בְּכַוָּונָה – כְּעֶבֶד בְּכַוָּונָה!
phrases.english: To include a slave killed by accident, like a slave killed on purpose!
And if you say that is indeed so,
but didn't Reish Lakish say:

phrases.aramaic: שׁוֹר שֶׁהֵמִית אֶת הָעֶבֶד שֶׁלֹּא בְּכַוָּונָה –
phrases.english: an ox that killed a slave by accident
is exempt from the thirty shekels!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יוחנן's reading from step 15
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's reading that 'אם כפר' includes an accidental killing
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same reading of 'אם עבד' would make the owner pay for a slave killed by accident, which goes against ריש לקיש's ruling.

steps.title: Two different אמוראים can disagree
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי answers אביי: you cannot attack רבי יוחנן's view with a ruling of ריש לקיש. Two different scholars can hold different opinions.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב דימי said to אביי: Are you setting one man against another man?!
steps.whatsHappening: רב דימי answers אביי's challenge from the previous step. He says that ריש לקיש's ruling does not prove anything about what רבי יוחנן holds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי argued that if 'אם' adds accidental cases, then a slave killed by accident should also cost thirty שקלים, and ריש לקיש says it does not. רב דימי answers that ריש לקיש may simply disagree with רבי יוחנן. So רבי יוחנן can consistently say the owner pays in both cases.

keyTerms.meaning: One man against another man, meaning a contradiction between two different scholars
You are setting against, raising a contradiction

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a common move in the גמרא: a contradiction only works when both statements come from the same person.

phrases.english: He said to him:
phrases.notes: רב דימי is answering אביי from the previous step.

phrases.english: Are you setting one man against another man?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's challenge in step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Separating the opinions: the contradiction comes from two different אמוראים who may disagree.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: ריש לקיש's ruling that the owner is exempt for an accidental slave killing seemed to disprove רבי יוחנן's reading of 'אם'.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יוחנן may hold that the owner pays even for an accidental slave killing. ריש לקיש simply disagrees.

steps.title: רבין reports that רבי יוחנן applies 'אם עבד' to accidental killing
steps.stepSummary: רבין confirms רב דימי's answer. רבי יוחנן learns from the extra word 'אם' that the owner pays thirty שקלים even when the ox killed a slave by accident.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבין came from ארץ ישראל, he said in the name of רבי יוחנן: The פסוק could have just said 'a slave'. Why does it say 'if a slave'? To include a slave killed by accident, treating it like a slave killed on purpose.
steps.whatsHappening: A new report from רבין supports what רב דימי just said. רבי יוחנן does hold that the owner pays for a slave killed by accident.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'אם' in 'אם עבד' looks extra. רבי יוחנן uses it to add the accidental case. This is the same method he used for 'אם כופר' in step 15, so his view is consistent.

keyTerms.meaning: When רבין came (from ארץ ישראל to בבל)
Why does the פסוק say this? (points out an extra word)
To include, to add a case
Not on purpose, by accident

phrases.english: When רבין came,
he said that רבי יוחנן said: [The פסוק could have said] 'a slave';
why does the פסוק say 'if a slave'?
To include a slave killed not on purpose,
like a slave killed on purpose.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתָא רָבִין אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Confirms רב דימי's answer: רבי יוחנן really does hold the owner liable for an accidental slave killing.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יוחנן, the extra word 'אם' in 'אם עבד' makes the owner pay thirty שקלים even when his ox killed a slave by accident.

steps.title: Suggesting that ריש לקיש rejects both extra words
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that ריש לקיש does not learn from 'אם עבד', so he also should not learn from 'אם כופר'. That would mean no כופר for an accidental killing.
steps.simpleTranslation: And for ריש לקיש too, let us say: since he does not learn anything from 'a slave' versus 'if a slave', he also does not learn anything from 'ransom' versus 'if ransom'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now turns to ריש לקיש and suggests a conclusion about his view. It infers his view on כופר from his view on the slave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ריש לקיש exempts the owner for an accidental slave killing, so he does not use 'אם עבד'. The suggestion is that he should be consistent and not use 'אם כופר' either. Then he would hold that no כופר is paid for an accidental killing.

keyTerms.meaning: Let us say (introduces a suggestion that may be rejected)
He learns a law from the wording of the פסוק
Ransom payment an ox owner makes when his ox kills a person

phrases.english: And for ריש לקיש too, let us say:
since he does not learn from 'a slave' versus 'if a slave',
he also does not learn from 'ransom' versus 'if ransom'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Having settled רבי יוחנן's view, the גמרא suggests a parallel conclusion for ריש לקיש.
steps.raayaObject: That according to ריש לקיש no כופר is paid when an ox kills a person by accident.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ריש לקיש's ruling that an ox that killed a slave by accident is exempt from thirty שקלים, which shows he does not learn from 'אם עבד'.

steps.title: ריש לקיש learns from 'אם כופר' but not from 'אם עבד'
steps.stepSummary: The suggestion is rejected. ריש לקיש may not learn from 'אם עבד', but he does learn from 'אם כופר', so כופר is paid even for an accidental killing.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: No. He does not learn from 'a slave' versus 'if a slave', but he does learn from 'ransom' versus 'if ransom'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the suggestion from the step before. It says ריש לקיש can treat the two words differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The suggestion assumed that whoever skips 'אם עבד' must also skip 'אם כופר'. The גמרא says this does not follow. ריש לקיש can learn from one extra 'אם' and not from the other. So even according to him, כופר may be paid for an accidental killing.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not assume this means ריש לקיש agrees about the slave. He still exempts the owner for an accidental slave killing. He only agrees that כופר is paid.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוחנן learns from both 'אם עבד' and 'אם כופר': the owner pays for an accidental killing in both cases. ריש לקיש learns only from 'אם כופר': he pays כופר but not the thirty שקלים for an accidental slave killing.

phrases.english: They said: No;
he does not learn from 'a slave' versus 'if a slave',
but he does learn from 'ransom' versus 'if ransom'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggestion of step 19.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the inference that ריש לקיש must treat 'אם כופר' the same way as 'אם עבד'.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The suggestion wrongly assumed that a scholar who does not learn from one extra 'אם' cannot learn from another.

steps.title: What is the difference between the two words 'אם'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why ריש לקיש treats 'אם עבד' and 'אם כופר' differently.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is the difference?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short question that sets up the next step. Why would ריש לקיש learn something from 'אם כופר' but not from 'אם עבד'?
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 20 the גמרא said ריש לקיש learns from 'אם כופר' but not from 'אם עבד'. Both phrases use the same word 'אם', so this looks inconsistent. The גמרא now asks for the reason.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difference? (a request to explain why two cases are treated differently)

phrases.english: And what is the difference?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the distinction drawn in Step 20.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why ריש לקיש learns from 'אם' by כופר but not by עבד.

steps.title: The word 'אם' by כופר sits in the payment part of the פסוק
steps.stepSummary: 'אם עבד' is part of describing the case, so the 'אם' is needed there. 'אם כופר' sits in the payment clause, so its 'אם' is extra and can teach something.
steps.simpleTranslation: With 'slave', the words 'if a slave' are not written in the place that talks about payment. With 'ransom', the words 'if a ransom' are written in the place that talks about payment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. The difference depends on where the word 'אם' appears in each פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'אם עבד יגח השור' describes what happened, and a case description naturally starts with 'if'. So that 'אם' is not extra. 'אם כופר יושת עליו' is the payment clause, and the פסוק could simply have said 'כופר יושת עליו'. That extra 'אם' teaches that כופר is paid even when the ox killed by accident.

keyTerms.meaning: A slave; here, the case of an ox that kills a slave
Ransom money paid by the owner of an ox that killed a person
In the place in the פסוק that talks about payment

steps.whatToRemember: ריש לקיש learns from 'אם' only when it is extra. In the payment clause by כופר it is extra, so כופר is paid even for an accidental killing. By עבד it is not extra, so there is no thirty שקלים for an accidental killing.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think ריש לקיש is being inconsistent about the word 'אם'. His rule is the same in both places. The word is extra in one פסוק and needed in the other.

phrases.english: 'Slave': 'if a slave'
is not written in the place of payment,
'Ransom': 'if a ransom'
is written in the place of payment.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 21.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The 'אם' by כופר is in the payment clause and is extra. The 'אם' by עבד is part of the case description and is needed.

steps.title: An ox that kills children: the owner is liable just as for adults
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא turns to the משנה's line 'and the same for a boy or a girl'. A ברייתא learns from the פסוק that the owner is liable for minors as for adults.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the same applies to a boy or a girl. The Rabbis taught: 'Whether it gored a son or gored a daughter.' This comes to make the owner liable for minors just as for adults.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line of the משנה. It brings a ברייתא showing the source in the פסוק that an ox killing a child is treated like an ox killing an adult.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'בן' and 'בת' in the פסוק refer to children. They teach that the laws of an ox that kills apply even when the victim is a minor. This is a new topic, separate from the עבד and כופר discussion.

keyTerms.meaning: A son or a daughter; here, a boy or girl who is a minor
Minors (children)
Adults

phrases.english: And so too with a boy or a girl.
The Rabbis taught:
'Whether it gored a son or gored a daughter':
to make him liable for minors as for adults.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן בְּבֵן אוֹ בְּבַת. תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic based on the next line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The owner of an ox that kills a minor is liable just as if it killed an adult. This is learned from 'או בן יגח או בת יגח'.

steps.title: Couldn't we learn this from a person who kills?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks why a פסוק is needed. Logic could compare an ox that kills to a person who kills, and a person who kills is liable whether the victim is a child or an adult.
steps.simpleTranslation: But couldn't this be learned by logic? The Torah makes a person liable for killing a person, and it makes an ox liable for killing a person. When a person kills a person, there is no difference between minors and adults. So too when an ox kills a person, do not make a difference between minors and adults!
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא challenges its own source. It argues the rule could be figured out by logic without a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both a person and an ox face death for killing a person. A person who kills is liable whether the victim is a child or an adult. So an ox should be treated the same way, and the פסוק 'בן או בת' seems unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it a logical argument? (could this not be learned by reasoning?)
Since
Do not make a difference

phrases.english: But isn't it a logical argument?
Since He made a person liable for a person,
phrases.notes: He means a person who kills another person gets the death penalty.

phrases.english: and He made an ox liable for a person;
just as when He made a person liable for a person,
there is no difference between minors and adults,
so too when He made an ox liable for a person,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא תַּחְלוֹק בּוֹ בֵּין קְטַנִּים לִגְדוֹלִים!
phrases.english: do not make a difference in it between minors and adults!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether the פסוק in Step 23 is needed.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for the פסוק 'או בן יגח או בת יגח'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A person who kills and an ox that kills are similar. A person is liable for killing minors and adults alike, so an ox should be too, even without a פסוק.

steps.title: A second argument: a קל וחומר begins
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא adds a stronger argument, a קל וחומר. A person who kills is liable for killing children even though children are not treated like adults in that area of law.
steps.simpleTranslation: And furthermore, it is a קל וחומר: a person who kills a person, where the Torah did not treat minors like adults, still makes him liable for minors as for adults;
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא begins a second, stronger logical argument. This step is only the first half. It sets up a conclusion that comes at the start of the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When it comes to people killing, minors are not treated like adults, because a child who kills is exempt. Even so, an adult who kills a child is fully liable. The ברייתא is building toward the point that an ox should surely be liable for killing a child, but that half comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: And furthermore; this adds another argument
An argument from a lighter case to a stricter case
That He did not make; the Torah did not treat them the same

phrases.english: And furthermore, it is a קל וחומר:
if with a person who kills a person,
where He did not make minors like adults,
He made him liable for minors as for adults;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second, stronger logical argument to the challenge in Step 24.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for the פסוק 'או בן יגח או בת יגח'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Even where minors are not treated like adults, a person is still liable for killing them. This sets up the argument that an ox should surely be liable for killing minors, which makes the פסוק seem unnecessary.
